blocks.content: The story starts with a problem nobody quite anticipated in 1981. IPv4 gave every device a unique 32-bit address, about 4.3 billion of them, and at the time that seemed like more than humanity could ever need. By the mid-1990s, it was obvious the internet would run out, growing far faster than anyone predicted.

NAT was the pragmatic hack that saved us. Firewalls are the deliberate wall that protects us. Together they form the invisible infrastructure behind every home router, every corporate network, and every cloud architecture running today. This topic covers exactly how NAT works, its real, honest limitations for system design, what a firewall actually does, and how the two combine in both a home router and a real cloud production architecture.
1. The IP Address Crisis: Why NAT Exists
blocks.text: 1. The IP Address Crisis: Why NAT Exists

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027095-519018335.png
blocks.alt: A fixed 4.3 billion addresses was never going to be enough for a world with billions of individually connected devices

blocks.content: The solution the internet landed on was designating certain IP ranges as private, usable freely inside any network but meaningless on the public internet itself, since they are never routed there at all.

Reserving these ranges only solves half the problem, an address that means nothing on the public internet still needs some mechanism to actually reach it, and that mechanism is exactly what NAT provides.
{"headers":["Private Range","Address Count"],"rows":[["10.0.0.0/8","About 16 million addresses"],["172.16.0.0/12","About 1 million addresses"],["192.168.0.0/16","65,536 addresses"]]}

A home network commonly uses 192.168.x.x, every phone, laptop, TV, and smart speaker gets its own private IP, while the router itself gets exactly one public IP from the internet provider. NAT is the technology that makes this arrangement actually work.
2. What NAT Actually Is
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273997549-154117938.png
blocks.alt: The router rewrites the source address on every outbound packet, so the outside world only ever sees the router's own public IP

blocks.content: Network Address Translation rewrites IP addresses on packets as they pass through a router. When a packet from a laptop's private address heads out to a destination like Google, the router replaces the source address with its own public IP before forwarding it. When the response comes back, the router translates in reverse, replacing the destination with the laptop's original private address, and forwards it home. To the outside world, an entire home network looks like a single device with a single IP.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273999329-800319578.png
blocks.alt: Multiple devices sharing one public IP are distinguished purely by which port number each one's connection is using

blocks.content: The router maintains a NAT table, a live mapping of every active connection. Three separate devices making three separate connections can all appear to come from the exact same public IP, distinguished entirely by different port numbers, a technique specifically called Port Address Translation, PAT.
3. Types of NAT
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274001047-942438734.png
blocks.alt: The three approaches trade permanence and public IP consumption differently

blocks.content: Static NAT creates a permanent, one-to-one mapping between a specific private IP and a specific public IP, exactly what a company reserves for an internal web server that must always be reachable from the same public address, regardless of who is asking.

Dynamic NAT also maps private addresses to public ones, but not permanently, the router draws from a pool of available public IPs, assigning one for the duration of a session and returning it to the pool once that session ends, so a different device can reuse the exact same public address later.

Port Address Translation, PAT, is what almost every home router actually uses today. Rather than assigning a separate public IP per device, it lets many devices share a single public IP simultaneously, tracking each one purely by the port number assigned to its own connection, letting thousands of devices communicate through one public IP without ever conflicting.
4. NAT Problems Every System Designer Encounters
blocks.text: 4. NAT Problems Every System Designer Encounters

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274002732-859058011.png
blocks.alt: NAT works cleanly when the private device initiates the connection, but an unsolicited inbound attempt has nowhere to go at all

blocks.content: NAT works great when the private device initiates a connection outward. But if someone on the internet tries to connect to a device behind NAT first, there is no NAT table entry for that attempt at all, and the packet has nowhere to go. This is exactly why two ordinary home devices cannot simply connect to each other directly, and why online gaming, video calls, and peer to peer file transfers all need special techniques to work at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274004403-124222780.png
blocks.alt: Both sides first learn their own public address through a shared server, then attempt a direct connection, falling back to a relay only if that fails

blocks.content: The fix is NAT traversal, techniques like STUN and TURN, along with hole punching. WebRTC, used in video calls, relies on exactly these, both devices first contact a public STUN server to learn their own public address, then attempt a direct connection using that information. When a direct connection genuinely cannot be established, the system falls back to a relay server, TURN, and this is precisely why real video call infrastructure has to maintain relay servers for the cases where direct connection simply fails.

NAT breaks the original internet design's assumption that every device has a unique, routable address and can connect directly to any other device. Many networking engineers consider this a genuine architectural flaw, exactly why IPv6, giving every device its own globally routable address, was designed to make NAT unnecessary altogether.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027283-943150588.png
blocks.alt: An idle connection's NAT table entry can expire before the connection itself is actually done, silently breaking it with no warning to either side

blocks.content: NAT is stateful, and that state can simply disappear. If a router reboots, or a connection sits idle long enough for its NAT table entry to time out, the connection dies silently. Long-lived TCP connections, database connections, SSH sessions, need their own keepalive packets specifically to prevent this, and a surprising number of real production database connection pool issues ultimately trace back to exactly this kind of NAT timeout.

Finally, logging and tracing get genuinely complicated behind NAT. Seeing one public IP make a suspicious request reveals nothing about which of the potentially hundreds of devices behind that same NAT actually sent it, correlating that back to a specific device requires the NAT's own logs at the exact matching timestamp.
5. What a Firewall Actually Is
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027286-938331454.png
blocks.alt: Rules are checked in order, the first match wins, and anything matching no rule at all is dropped by default

blocks.content: NAT is about address translation. A firewall is about access control, deciding which traffic is allowed through and which gets dropped outright. A firewall inspects packets and makes allow or deny decisions based on its own configured rules, sitting at network boundaries, between a private network and the internet, or between separate internal segments.

Firewall rules are processed top to bottom, and the first matching rule wins. Nearly every firewall ends with a default deny, anything not explicitly allowed is dropped, the principle of least privilege applied directly to network traffic.

This ordering matters in practice, a broad allow rule placed too early in the list can silently override a more specific deny rule meant to come first, exactly the kind of misconfiguration that quietly defeats an otherwise well-designed rule set.
6. Types of Firewalls
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274009517-638997130.png
blocks.alt: Each type inspects traffic at a different depth, trading simplicity for the ability to catch more sophisticated attacks

blocks.content: A packet filter, or stateless firewall, is the simplest kind, checking each packet independently using only its source IP, destination IP, port, and protocol, with no memory of any previous packet at all. A stateful firewall tracks active connections and remembers their state, distinguishing a packet belonging to an already-established, legitimate connection from a genuinely new connection attempt, meaningfully more secure than a stateless filter.

An application layer firewall, commonly called a Web Application Firewall or Layer 7 firewall, inspects the actual application data itself, not just packet headers, understanding protocols like HTTP, DNS, and SMTP well enough to detect attacks such as SQL injection or cross-site scripting hidden inside otherwise ordinary-looking traffic.
7. DMZ: Tying NAT and Firewalls Together
blocks.text: 7. DMZ: Tying NAT and Firewalls Together

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027286-420293106.png
blocks.alt: Public-facing servers live in an isolated middle zone, so a compromise there never automatically reaches the truly internal network

blocks.content: A DMZ, demilitarized zone, is a network segment sitting between the internet and an internal private network. Servers that must be reachable from the internet, web servers, mail servers, DNS servers, live in the DMZ, while databases, internal tools, and employee machines live in the genuinely internal network, with two firewalls, or one firewall with three separate interfaces, enforcing both boundaries.

The first firewall allows only the specific ports the DMZ's own public-facing servers genuinely need, port 443 and 80 to the web server, port 25 to the mail server, denying everything else by default.

The logic is simple: if your web server gets compromised, the attacker should not be able to directly reach your database. A second firewall between the DMZ and the internal network exists specifically to guarantee that.
8. How Your Home Router Actually Works
blocks.text: 8. How Your Home Router Actually Works

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027622-842467266.png
blocks.alt: NAT's own table lookup requirement means an unsolicited inbound connection has no entry to match, and gets dropped as a pure side effect

blocks.content: A home router is simultaneously doing NAT and firewalling, though most people never realize these are two entirely separate functions running on the same box. There is a genuinely important side effect of NAT that most people miss entirely, NAT provides implicit inbound protection for free. When someone on the internet tries to connect directly to a device's private IP, they simply cannot, that address is not routable at all. Even targeting the public IP directly, the router has no NAT table entry for an unsolicited inbound connection, so it drops the packet, this is why home devices are generally not directly exploitable from the open internet, NAT acts as an accidental firewall.

blocks.title: This Is Not a Real Substitute for a Firewall
blocks.content: NAT's accidental protection only ever covers unsolicited inbound connections. If malware already running on a device initiates a connection outbound itself, NAT happily creates a table entry and lets that connection succeed, exactly like any other legitimate outbound request. NAT protects against the outside reaching in uninvited, nothing more.

The example below implements exactly the core mechanism behind NAT's accidental protection: a small NAT table that correctly translates a genuine response back to the private device that actually asked for it, while an unsolicited inbound packet targeting a port with no matching table entry at all is correctly dropped.

codes.python:
class NatTable:
    # A simplified NAT table: outbound connections are assigned a public port and
    # recorded, so a genuine response can be routed back to the right private
    # device, while an unsolicited inbound packet with no matching entry is dropped.
    def __init__(self):
        self.port_to_private_endpoint = {}
        self.next_public_port = 54321

    def translate_outbound(self, private_ip, private_port, destination):
        public_port = str(self.next_public_port)
        self.next_public_port += 1
        self.port_to_private_endpoint[public_port] = f"{private_ip}:{private_port}"
        return public_port

    def translate_inbound(self, public_port):
        private_endpoint = self.port_to_private_endpoint.get(public_port)
        if private_endpoint is None:
            return "DROPPED, no NAT table entry exists for this port"
        return private_endpoint


def main():
    nat = NatTable()

    public_port_a = nat.translate_outbound("192.168.1.5", 49823, "8.8.8.8:443")
    print(f"Device A's outbound connection assigned public port {public_port_a}")

    public_port_b = nat.translate_outbound("192.168.1.7", 51002, "1.1.1.1:443")
    print(f"Device B's outbound connection assigned public port {public_port_b}")

    response_for = nat.translate_inbound(public_port_a)
    print(f"Response arrives for port {public_port_a}, forwarded to: {response_for}")

    unsolicited = nat.translate_inbound("54999")
    print(f"Unsolicited inbound attempt on port 54999: {unsolicited}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: 9. NAT and Firewalls in Cloud Environments
blocks.text: 9. NAT and Firewalls in Cloud Environments

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027623-879201892.png
blocks.alt: The standard production pattern: only the load balancer and NAT gateway are public, application servers and the database never are

blocks.content: In AWS, GCP, and Azure, NAT and firewalls still exist, but look genuinely different from a home router. Security Groups are stateful firewalls attached directly to each individual instance, defining exactly which ports accept inbound traffic and from which sources. Network ACLs are stateless packet filters applied at the subnet level instead, processing rules in order with entirely separate inbound and outbound lists, and are far less commonly configured by hand than Security Groups.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274016603-974160673.png
blocks.alt: Security Groups protect at the instance level and remember connection state, NACLs protect at the subnet level and do not

blocks.content: A NAT Gateway is a fully managed NAT device for private subnets, letting instances with no public IP of their own still reach the internet outbound, for downloading patches or calling external APIs, entirely through the gateway's own public address.

The standard production pattern: users reach a load balancer sitting in a public subnet, reachable from the internet. The load balancer forwards to application servers in a private subnet, with no public IPs of their own at all. Those app servers connect to a database reachable only from their own security group, and reach the internet outbound, when genuinely needed, only through a NAT Gateway.
10. Common System Design Interview Questions

["How do you secure your backend servers? Place them in a private subnet with no public IPs, reachable only through a load balancer, with security groups at every layer restricting exactly what each layer accepts","How do private instances download software updates with no public IP? Through a NAT Gateway sitting in the public subnet, routing only outbound traffic, nothing from the internet can initiate a connection back in through it","How do you prevent SQL injection and cross-site scripting? A stateful firewall or security group alone cannot, they never inspect the actual HTTP payload, a Web Application Firewall in front of the application is what actually catches this","How does your architecture handle a DDoS attack? In layers, volumetric bandwidth flooding absorbed at the network edge by the provider or CDN, excessive connection attempts rate limited at the load balancer itself"]

How do private instances download software updates with no public IP? Through a NAT Gateway sitting in the public subnet, routing only outbound traffic, nothing from the internet can initiate a connection back in through it

How do you prevent SQL injection and cross-site scripting? A stateful firewall or security group alone cannot, they never inspect the actual HTTP payload, a Web Application Firewall in front of the application is what actually catches this

blocks.content: 11. Port Forwarding: Deliberately Opening a Hole
blocks.text: 11. Port Forwarding: Deliberately Opening a Hole

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027625-411301207.png
blocks.alt: A port forwarding rule deliberately overrides NAT's own accidental protection for one specific, chosen port

blocks.content: Sometimes a device behind NAT genuinely needs to accept unsolicited inbound connections, self-hosting a game server, or running a personal web server from home. Port forwarding lets a router owner configure a fixed rule saying any inbound traffic on a specific port should always be forwarded to one specific private device, deliberately punching a permanent hole through NAT's own accidental protection for that single port.

blocks.title: A Deliberate, Narrow Exception
blocks.content: Port forwarding should always be scoped to exactly the one port genuinely needed, opening more than that meaningfully increases the exposed attack surface of whatever device sits behind it.
12. Carrier-Grade NAT
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274020008-62346594.png
blocks.alt: Some home routers are themselves behind another layer of NAT run by the internet provider, translating twice before reaching the real internet

blocks.content: Some internet providers, particularly for mobile and some residential connections, do not actually give a home router a genuine public IP at all, they assign it another private-range address and run their own large-scale NAT, Carrier-Grade NAT, translating it again before traffic reaches the real public internet. This double layer of NAT makes port forwarding and NAT traversal meaningfully harder, since the home router's own public-looking IP is not actually reachable from the internet on its own at all.
13. IPv6: Removing the Need for NAT Entirely
blocks.text: 13. IPv6: Removing the Need for NAT Entirely

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027287-699387569.png
blocks.alt: With effectively unlimited addresses, every device can have its own genuine public address, removing the entire reason NAT exists

blocks.content: NAT exists purely because IPv4 addresses are scarce. IPv6, covered in depth in the IP Addressing topic, has such an enormous address space that every single device can have its own genuine, globally routable public address, removing the entire motivating reason for NAT to exist at all. Firewalls remain just as necessary under IPv6, access control is a separate concern entirely, but the specific problems NAT introduces, asymmetric connectivity, NAT traversal complexity, translation table timeouts, simply do not apply once every device has its own real address.
14. A Common Mistake: Treating NAT as a Real Firewall
blocks.text: 14. A Common Mistake: Treating NAT as a Real Firewall

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027620-676191260.png
blocks.alt: NAT's accidental protection only ever covers unsolicited inbound traffic, it does nothing once something inside has already initiated an outbound connection itself

blocks.content: A genuinely common misconception is believing that sitting behind NAT alone is meaningful security. It only ever blocks unsolicited inbound connections. If malware is already running on a device behind that same NAT, it can freely initiate its own outbound connection, and NAT creates a table entry for it exactly like any other legitimate request, providing zero protection against that scenario at all.
A genuinely secure home or corporate network layers a real, deliberately configured firewall on top of NAT's own accidental side effect, rather than assuming NAT alone is a substitute for one.
Worked Example

A team deploys a standard three-tier architecture on AWS: a load balancer in a public subnet accepting traffic from the internet on ports 80 and 443, application servers in a private subnet with security groups accepting connections only from the load balancer's own security group, and a database reachable only from the app servers' security group specifically, not from the load balancer or the internet at all.

If an attacker ever manages to compromise the load balancer itself, this layered structure still means they cannot reach the database directly, they would need to separately compromise an application server first, exactly the same structural benefit a DMZ provides between a public-facing web server and an internal network.

When the app servers need to call an external payment API or download a security patch, that outbound traffic routes through a NAT Gateway in the public subnet, which itself accepts no inbound connections from the internet whatsoever, only ever forwarding traffic the private instances themselves initiated.
Common Mistakes

["Treating NAT's accidental inbound protection as an actual substitute for a real, deliberately configured firewall","Forgetting that long-lived connections like database sessions need their own keepalive packets to survive an idle NAT table timeout","Assuming a stateful firewall or security group alone can catch application-layer attacks like SQL injection, when only a WAF actually inspects payloads that deeply","Placing a database or internal tool directly in a public subnet instead of a private one behind application servers, removing the entire point of the layered architecture"]
items: Treating NAT's accidental inbound protection as an actual substitute for a real, deliberately configured firewall
Forgetting that long-lived connections like database sessions need their own keepalive packets to survive an idle NAT table timeout
Assuming a stateful firewall or security group alone can catch application-layer attacks like SQL injection, when only a WAF actually inspects payloads that deeply
Placing a database or internal tool directly in a public subnet instead of a private one behind application servers, removing the entire point of the layered architecture

blocks.content: Practice

Sketch a three-tier cloud architecture: a public subnet with a load balancer and NAT Gateway, a private subnet with application servers, and a database reachable only from those app servers. For each connection in the diagram, state explicitly which security group or NACL rule allows it, and what happens to any other connection attempt not explicitly covered.
Then explain, in your own words, exactly why a long-lived SSH session over a home NAT connection can silently die after sitting idle for a while, and what specific technique prevents it.

As a third exercise, explain why a friend trying to host a small personal game server at home would need to configure port forwarding specifically, and what security consideration they should weigh before opening that one port to the entire internet.
Key Takeaway

NAT was a pragmatic hack extending IPv4's life by letting many private devices share a small pool of public IPs, working by rewriting addresses and tracking connections through a translation table, most commonly by port. Firewalls are deliberate access control, ranging from simple stateless packet filters to connection-aware stateful firewalls to payload-inspecting application layer firewalls. In real system design, the pattern is consistent: public-facing components sit in a public subnet, application logic sits in a private subnet with no direct internet exposure, and NAT combined with layered firewalls is what actually shapes which services can reach what, and what the outside world can never reach directly at all.

Neither NAT nor a firewall is interesting purely on its own, they matter because together they define the actual shape of what any real architecture can and cannot do, which services are reachable from where, and what stays permanently invisible to the outside world by design.
